## Definition

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i
e j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j
e i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E	o\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $
u=(
u_i)_{i\in E}$, meaning $
u_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in E}
u_i=1$; initial law $
u$ means $\mathbb P(Y_0=i)=
u_i$ for every $i\in E$. Put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and set $N_t=0$ for every $t\ge0$ and let the associated realization be the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim
u$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $
u$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain-existence]] proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

## Example

On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$ and fix plus boundary spins $\sigma_x=+1$ whenever $\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n$. For $\sigma_x\in\{-1,+1\}$, define the finite-volume Ising Hamiltonian and Gibbs law by
$$H_{I,n}(\sigma)=-J_I\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\sigma_x\sigma_y,\qquad \mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma)\propto e^{-\beta H_{I,n}(\sigma)},\quad J_I>0.$$
Define $m_I^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma_0=+1)-1/2$ when the limit exists, and $\beta_c^I:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_I^+(\beta)>0\}$. The limit exists and
$$\beta_c^I J_I=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2).$$

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For each finite box and edge, [F1] gives $-J_P\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}=-(J_P/2)\sigma_x\sigma_y-J_P/2$. Setting $J_P=2J_I$ makes the finite Potts Hamiltonian equal to $H_{I,n}(\sigma)-J_I|E_n|$. The difference is independent of $\sigma$, so it cancels from the normalized finite Gibbs probabilities. The boundary color $1$ in the Potts model corresponds to the Ising plus spin $+1$. Thus the two models have the same plus-boundary probabilities and the same critical inverse temperature. [F1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Let $\beta_c^P$ and $\beta_c^I$ denote the critical inverse temperatures in the two definitions. Step 1.1 gives $\beta_c^I=\beta_c^P$. By [F2] with $J_P=2J_I$, $\beta_c^P(2J_I)=\log(1+\sqrt2)$. Divide by $2$ to obtain $\beta_c^I J_I=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$. This is an exact coupling conversion; the constant energy shift does not affect probabilities. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $q\geq1$, put $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. The square-lattice free and wired cylinder-limit FK probability laws exist. For every $p>p_{\rm sd}(q)$, both have positive percolation probability. For every $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$, there are $C(p,q),c(p,q)>0$ such that every arbitrary-boundary cylinder-limit FK state $\phi$ satisfies
$$\phi(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z^2).$$
In particular, both percolation probabilities vanish below $p_{\rm sd}(q)$ and $p_c^0(q)=p_c^1(q)=p_{\rm sd}(q)$. These conclusions do not identify the free and wired measures at the critical parameter.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 By [A1] and [F1] the free and wired probability laws exist. In either law the events $D_r$ decrease with $r$. Their intersection is precisely the event that the origin cluster is unbounded: connection to every box boundary is equivalent to an unbounded cluster, and every finite path reaching a farther boundary contains an initial path to the nearer boundary. Countable additivity gives continuity from above, hence $\theta^b(p,q)=\inf_r\pi^b_p(D_r)=\Theta^b(p)$. This uses actual existing probability laws, rather than inferring their existence from consistent numerical cylinder weights. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Fix $p>p_{\rm sd}(q)$ and set $t=(p+p_{\rm sd}(q))/2$. Then $p_{\rm sd}(q)<t<p$. By [F2] and [F3], $\Theta^0(p)\geq\Theta^1(t)>0$, while [F3] directly gives $\Theta^1(p)>0$. Step 1.1 proves positive percolation for both laws at $p$. No equality of free and wired laws is used. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 For $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$ apply [F4]. In particular, each free or wired law satisfies the displayed bound. An origin path to $\partial\Lambda_r$ reaches one of its $8r$ vertices, each of Euclidean norm at least $r$. A finite union bound gives $\phi(D_r)\leq8rC(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)r}\to0$. Step 1.1 then gives zero percolation. Both defining infima are $p_{\rm sd}(q)$, since every parameter above it belongs to each positive-percolation set and none below it does. The bound for all other cylinder-limit states is already exactly [F4]. [F4, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 Form the quotient vertex set $V_\xi$ by identifying each $\xi$-class. For an edge with distinct quotient endpoints $u,v$, let its incidence vector be $e_u+e_v\in\mathbb F_2^{V_\xi}$; a quotient loop has zero vector. In a component $C$ of the opened quotient graph $(V_\xi,A)$, every edge vector has even coordinate sum, so their span lies in the even-sum subspace, of dimension $|C|-1$. Conversely choose a root $r\in C$. For every $v\in C\setminus\{r\}$, connectedness [F2] gives an open path from $r$ to $v$; summing its edge vectors over $\mathbb F_2$ cancels each internal vertex twice and gives $e_r+e_v$. These $|C|-1$ vectors are linearly independent by their distinct $v$-coordinates. Thus the incidence rank on $C$ is $|C|-1$, and summing over components gives $r(A)=|V_\xi|-k_\xi(A)$, including isolated vertices and quotient loops. If $U_A$ and $U_C$ are the spans of incidence vectors from edge sets $A$ and $C$, then $U_{A\cup C}=U_A+U_C$ and $U_{A\cap C}\subseteq U_A\cap U_C$. The subspace dimension formula therefore gives $r(A)+r(C)\geq r(A\cup C)+r(A\cap C)$, hence $k_\xi(A\cup C)+k_\xi(A\cap C)\geq k_\xi(A)+k_\xi(C)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
support_paragraphs.1.2: 1.2 Fix the exterior edge states outside a finite $F\subseteq E$. For an interior edge set $A\subseteq F$, the total number of components of the combined graph is the number of exterior-only components disjoint from the boundary of $F$, plus the number of components of the graph on $F$ after identifying its boundary vertices that are connected by the fixed exterior open edges or by $\xi$. The first summand and all exterior edge factors are constant in $A$; they cancel when the conditional weights are normalized. Hence the conditional law on $F$ is exactly the finite FK law with this induced boundary partition. [F1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Since $|A\cup C|+|A\cap C|=|A|+|C|$, the factors $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}$ have equality in the lattice condition. The component inequality in step 1.1 and $q\geq1$ give the displayed log-supermodular inequality; every mass is positive by $0<p<1$ and $q\geq1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.2: 2.2 Given all edges except $e$, let $s$ be the conditional number of components when $e$ is closed. If its endpoints are already connected, opening it leaves $s$ unchanged, so open-to-closed odds are $p/(1-p)$ and the open probability is $p$. If the endpoints are not connected, opening it changes the component factor from $q^s$ to $q^{s-1}$, so the odds are $p/[q(1-p)]$ and the open probability is $p/(p+q(1-p))$. Both expressions increase with $p$; opening other edges or making the boundary partition coarser can only turn the second case into the first. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

For the last coordinate $s\in\{0,1\}$, each conditional measure $\mu_s$ on the first $n-1$ coordinates remains log-supermodular, so induction makes each $\mu_s$ positively associated. The ratio $R(x)=\mu(X_n=1,x)/\mu(X_n=0,x)$ is increasing in $x$: for $x\leq y$, apply log-supermodularity to $(y,0)$ and $(x,1)$ to obtain $R(y)\geq R(x)$. Thus for every increasing $h$, $\mathbb E_{\mu_1}h=\mathbb E_{\mu_0}(hR)/\mathbb E_{\mu_0}R\geq\mathbb E_{\mu_0}h$ by positive association under $\mu_0$. For increasing $f,g$, their conditional means $F_s=\mathbb E[f\mid X_n=s]$ and $G_s=\mathbb E[g\mid X_n=s]$ therefore satisfy $F_1\geq F_0$ and $G_1\geq G_0$. The conditional association and the nonnegative covariance of two increasing functions of the single Bernoulli coordinate give $\mathbb E(fg)\geq\sum_s\mu(X_n=s)F_sG_s\geq\mathbb E f\,\mathbb E g$. [step 2.1, algebra, induction]

Each update resamples one edge from its conditional FK law, so it preserves the corresponding FK law. Step 2.2 makes every coupled update preserve coordinatewise order. To prove marginal convergence, fix $j\in\{1,2\}$ and couple two copies of the chain with this same fixed kernel $(p_j,q,\xi_j)$, one from any configuration and one from its stationary FK law. If there are $r>0$ labels, a block of $r$ updates chooses them in a prescribed order with probability $r^{-r}$. If all its uniforms exceed $p_2<1$, every label is closed at the block end in both copies, regardless of their initial configurations. This event has probability $\delta=r^{-r}(1-p_2)^r>0$. Once these same-kernel copies meet they remain equal under shared updates. Independence of the update blocks bounds their disagreement probability after $k$ blocks by $(1-\delta)^k$, proving convergence of each marginal to its FK law. No absorbing equality is claimed between the different-kernel chains. For every increasing real $f$ on the finite configuration space, their order at every time gives $\mathbb E f(X_t^{(1)})\leq\mathbb E f(X_t^{(2)})$; taking the two marginal limits proves stochastic domination. When $r=0$ there is one configuration and the conclusion is immediate. [step 2.2, construct, algebra] ∎

Let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, $J>0$, and $\beta>0$. On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n\}$ and let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$. The $Q$-state Potts model has spins $\sigma:\Lambda_n\to\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, fixed plus boundary $\sigma|_{B_n}=1$, and finite-volume Gibbs probabilities proportional to $e^{-\beta H_n(\sigma)}$, where
$$H_n(\sigma)=-J\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}.$$
Define its plus-boundary order parameter by
$$m_Q^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^+(\sigma_0=1)-Q^{-1},$$
when the limit exists, and define $\beta_c:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_Q^+(\beta)>0\}$. Then the limit exists and
$$\beta_c J=\log(1+\sqrt Q).$$
This is a numerical limit of finite-volume probabilities; no infinite-volume probability-law extension is required.

1.1 Put $v=e^{\beta J}-1$ and $p=v/(1+v)=1-e^{-\beta J}$. On the finite spin-edge configurations with $\sigma|_{B_n}=1$, define the joint weight

For fixed $\sigma$, summing over $A\subseteq E_n$ gives $\prod_{e\in E_n}(1+v\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}})=e^{-\beta H_n(\sigma)}$.
